# Education in China – Concise Summary
Education in China has undergone significant transformation since 1949, evolving from a focus on improving literacy and promoting social equality to one centered on economic modernization, scientific advancement, and national competitiveness. The system comprises nine years of compulsory education (six years of primary and three years of junior secondary), followed by optional senior secondary schooling—academic or vocational. Primary education emphasizes Chinese, mathematics, and moral training, with disparities between urban and rural access and quality. A range of reforms has aimed to universalize education, promote inclusion, reduce homework burdens, and address regional and socioeconomic inequalities; notable policies include the "Double Reduction Policy" and the establishment of standardized curricula and teacher qualifications.
China’s secondary and higher education systems have expanded rapidly, with competitive examinations (Zhongkao and Gaokao) determining advancement to selective schools and universities. Vocational education is encouraged to meet market demands for skilled labor. Higher education has grown to over 3,000 institutions and more than 44 million students, featuring elite universities, international exchange, and government-led initiatives such as the Double First-Class Construction. Adult and online education are significant, allowing continued learning and retraining. Despite impressive academic achievement internationally, challenges persist—regional and gender gaps, education stress, teacher shortages, and criticisms of rote learning and limited innovation. Education is highly politicized, with curriculum censorship and mandatory courses in Marxism and Chinese Communist Party history permeating all levels.
